--- title: "Lab 2: Evaluation: Metrics and Cross-Validation" subtitle: "FW 532 · Python version" --- **Goals:** * To understand what each of a set of common evaluation metrics measures, how the metrics do/don't depend on the prediction threshold, and how to compute them in Python. * To implement several cross-validation strategies and explore trade-offs within and among them. **You Will Need:** * The course environmental raster stack (`data/envStack.tif`, included in the starter kit) * Python packages: numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, rasterio (see `requirements.txt`) * The course helper module `sdmlab.py` (in the same folder as this notebook) Remember to run the cells in order, from top to bottom. ::: {#efb4a42d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Running on Google Colab? This cell downloads the course files. (Anywhere else it does nothing.) import os, sys if "google.colab" in sys.modules: if not os.path.exists("/content/fw532"): !git clone -q --depth 1 https://github.com/Hutchinson-Lab/fw532.git /content/fw532 %pip install -q rasterio os.chdir("/content/fw532/python") ``` ::: First, load the packages we need. Besides numpy, pandas, matplotlib, and statsmodels (from Lab 1), this lab uses **scikit-learn** (`sklearn`), Python's main machine-learning library, for ROC and precision-recall curves and for cross-validation folds. `from ... import ...` lets us use a few functions by their short names. ::: {#394076ff .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy.stats import norm from sklearn.metrics import (roc_curve, roc_auc_score, auc, precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score) from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold import sdmlab as sdm # course helpers for rasters and evaluation env_stack = sdm.load_env() ``` ::: # SET-UP In the last lab, you simulated some data and fit at least one model. You looked at parameter estimates and the predicted probability surface for the simulated species. Since it was simulated, we could directly ask how well the fitted model estimated the parameter values. Of course, in reality, you don't already know how the data were generated - this is why you're fitting a model! In this lab, we will dig into different ways to measure the quality of your model. To set up, we'll create a simulated data set again. We'll divide it into two pieces: a "training set" for fitting the model, and a "testing set" for evaluating the model. At first, we'll divide it arbitrarily, and in the second part of the lab, we'll look at other possible set-ups. # Simulate Data This block simulates presence/absence data, for which we'll look at a suite of evaluation metrics. ::: {#89020578 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # define logistic function def logistic(x): return np.exp(x) / (1 + np.exp(x)) # scale the climate variables (each layer gets mean 0 and standard deviation 1, as in Lab 1): env_stack = env_stack.scale() # get points n_points = 500 # n_points = 3000 sim_pts = env_stack.sample_random(n_points, seed=1234) # set parameters intercept = -1.5 beta1 = -1.5 beta2 = -1.5 beta3 = 1.5 p_occ_raster = logistic(intercept + beta1 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Precipitation.Seasonality"]) + beta2 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month"]) + beta3 * sdm.scale(env_stack["Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"])) # get the values that correspond to the points we selected: p_occs = sdm.extract(p_occ_raster, env_stack, sim_pts["x"], sim_pts["y"]) # sample from these probabilities (a *different* seed than above -- see Lab 1): rng = np.random.default_rng(5678) pres_abs = rng.binomial(n=1, p=p_occs) # put response and variables together in a DataFrame: modeling_df = sim_pts.copy() modeling_df.insert(0, "presAbs", pres_abs) # plot the result ax = sdm.plot_map(p_occ_raster, env_stack, title="pOcc") present = modeling_df["presAbs"] == 1 ax.scatter(modeling_df.loc[present, "x"], modeling_df.loc[present, "y"], s=8, color="red", label="detection") ax.scatter(modeling_df.loc[~present, "x"], modeling_df.loc[~present, "y"], s=8, color="blue", label="non-detection") ax.legend(loc="center left"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=531 height=292} ::: ::: (`~` means "not": `~present` is True for the absences.) Let's make half of these training points and half test points at random. (`sample_random()` returns the points in random order, so the first half and the second half are each a random sample.) `n_points // 2` is integer division (500 // 2 = 250), and `.iloc[a:b]` selects rows by position. ::: {#22e89338 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} train_data = modeling_df.iloc[:n_points // 2] test_data = modeling_df.iloc[n_points // 2:] ``` ::: # Fit a basic model Now you can fit a simple model to these data. Let's suppose your model is not perfect - you fail to include "Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month" and instead include "Precipitation.of.Coldest.Quarter." Using this model, you can get predicted probabilities for the test points. ::: {#c10b99f4 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} model1_vars = ["Precipitation.Seasonality", "Precipitation.of.Coldest.Quarter", # "Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"] model1 = sm.GLM(train_data["presAbs"], sm.add_constant(train_data[model1_vars]), family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit() pred_probs = model1.predict(sm.add_constant(test_data[model1_vars])) pd.DataFrame({"pred": pred_probs.round(2), "truth": test_data["presAbs"]}).head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
pred truth
250 0.08 0
251 0.26 1
252 0.44 1
253 0.12 0
254 0.02 0
``` ::: ::: Now your model has made some predictions about the test points on the probability scale. Your test data includes 0s for absences and 1s for presences. Your task is to choose how to measure the agreement (or lack thereof) between your model predictions and the test data. # PART 1: METRICS # Thresholded metrics As you go through this section, you might find this to be a useful reference: [Classifier evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_of_binary_classifiers) One option is to threshold the predictions to turn them into 0s and 1s like the response variable in your test data. To do this, you must choose a threshold. For starters, use 0.5, since it is halfway between 0 and 1. ::: {#b0d0f1c5 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} thresh = 0.5 # set the threshold logical_preds = pred_probs > thresh # threshold the predictions (True/False) binary_preds = logical_preds.astype(int) # convert to binary (1/0) instead of logical pd.DataFrame({"pred": pred_probs.round(2), "truth": test_data["presAbs"], "binary_preds": binary_preds}).head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
pred truth binary_preds
250 0.08 0 0
251 0.26 1 0
252 0.44 1 0
253 0.12 0 0
254 0.02 0 0
``` ::: ::: Now you can use a confusion matrix to compare the predictions to the observations. A confusion matrix has four cells. In R, the caret package computes confusion matrices and a suite of summary metrics for them. The course helper `sdm.confusion_summary()` reports the same statistics (everything caret prints except McNemar's test). `help()` shows a function's documentation, and you can open `sdmlab.py` to see exactly how each number is computed: ::: {#1e22f876 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} help(sdm.confusion_summary) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Help on function confusion_summary in module sdmlab: confusion_summary(y_true, y_pred, positive=1, show=True) -> 'dict' Confusion matrix plus the summary statistics reported by caret::confusionMatrix. ``` ::: ::: Here is our first confusion matrix and associated metrics. The function takes the true labels and the thresholded predictions; presences (1) are treated as the "positive" class. ::: {#b9d7ce8f .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} cm = sdm.confusion_summary(test_data["presAbs"], binary_preds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Confusion matrix (rows = prediction, columns = truth) true 0 true 1 pred 0 171 38 pred 1 14 27 Accuracy : 0.7920 95% CI : (0.7364, 0.8406) No Information Rate : 0.7400 P-Value [Acc > NIR] : 0.0335 Kappa : 0.3859 Sensitivity : 0.4154 Specificity : 0.9243 Pos Pred Value : 0.6585 Neg Pred Value : 0.8182 Prevalence : 0.2600 Detection Rate : 0.1080 Detection Prevalence : 0.1640 Balanced Accuracy : 0.6699 ``` ::: ::: (Note that this arrangement of the cells, with predictions in rows and the truth in columns, is the same as caret's and different from the wikipedia page.) Please make sure you understand at least: accuracy, no information rate, kappa, sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value. Note that many of these have more than one name! You can cross-reference with the Wikipedia page. `cm` is a *dictionary*: a set of named values. `cm["Kappa"]` gets one of them. Another metric that you may see in ecology but is not automatically computed here is the True Skill Statistic (TSS) = Sensitivity + Specificity - 1 (e.g., Allouche et al (2006) below). Let's compute sensitivity and specificity by hand from the predictions, to see exactly what they are. (`&` means "and"; `np.sum()` of True/False values counts the Trues.) ::: {#baca1ab5 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} y_test = test_data["presAbs"] sens = np.sum((binary_preds == 1) & (y_test == 1)) / np.sum(y_test == 1) # TP / all presences spec = np.sum((binary_preds == 0) & (y_test == 0)) / np.sum(y_test == 0) # TN / all absences print(sens, cm["Sensitivity"]) # same as the helper's values print(spec, cm["Specificity"]) tss = sens + spec - 1 tss ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.4153846153846154 0.4153846153846154 0.9243243243243243 0.9243243243243243 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` np.float64(0.3397089397089397) ``` ::: ::: There are many choices here for measuring success with binary outcomes (i.e., presence/absence data)! You are encouraged to think about which of these might be most relevant for different modeling scenarios. Which is the best characterization of model success for your project? All of the above has compared binary predictions to binary true values, where the binary predictions were created by thresholding model outputs between 0 and 1. Therefore, the confusion matrix and associated metrics will change as the threshold varies. You can prove this to yourself by trying a different threshold. There are a variety of ways to choose your threshold. Once again, there are choices in how to set the threshold. You could use information from the training data. For example, you could take the fitted probabilities on the training data and use the minimum probability among all positive training points, so that the model would predict all the positives correctly on the training data. ::: {#94a78ab1 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} train_fitted = model1.fittedvalues # fitted probabilities for the training points min_train_pres_thresh = train_fitted[train_data["presAbs"] == 1].min() min_train_pres_thresh ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` np.float64(0.06276924739389898) ``` ::: ::: Or, you could ask to predict 90% of the training positives correctly, etc. ::: {#832088dd .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ninety_percent_pres_thresh = np.quantile(train_fitted[train_data["presAbs"] == 1], 0.1) ninety_percent_pres_thresh ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` np.float64(0.20007647561332384) ``` ::: ::: Or just use the training set prevalence: here, the proportion of 0s in the training data (1 - prevalence). ::: {#54511f9d .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} train_prev_thresh = 1 - train_data["presAbs"].mean() train_prev_thresh ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` np.float64(0.708) ``` ::: ::: Another approach would be to choose the threshold based on sensitivity and specificity (e.g. the threshold at which they are equal, the threshold that maximizes their sum). This entails searching through a set of thresholds. > **Exercise 1:** Choose one of these alternate thresholds and compute the metrics again. Report > what threshold you chose and comment on your results. # Threshold-independent metrics Alternatively, you may wish to avoid all this thresholding business. ROC curves plot performance across all possible thresholds. The area under these curves summarizes performance into threshold-independent measures. scikit-learn's `roc_curve()` computes the curve: for every threshold, the false positive rate (FPR = 1 - specificity) and the true positive rate (TPR = sensitivity). We plot FPR on the x-axis, running from 0 to 1. (R's pROC package instead puts specificity on the x-axis, running from 1 down to 0. It is the same curve.) The R version of this lab also adds two things to the plot: * **A smoothed curve.** pROC's `smooth()` assumes the scores of presences and absences are both normally distributed after some transformation (the "binormal" model). Then the ROC curve is a straight line when sensitivity and specificity are put on the normal-quantile (probit) scale. We can do the same: transform with `norm.ppf()`, fit a line with `np.polyfit()`, and transform back with `norm.cdf()`. * **Confidence intervals.** pROC's `ci(of = "thresholds")` resamples the test points with replacement (a *bootstrap*) many times and draws error bars for sensitivity and specificity at selected thresholds. Below we do a similar bootstrap and draw a grey band showing, at each FPR, the middle 95% of the bootstrapped sensitivities. The idea is the same, but the band is not identical to pROC's error bars. ::: {#93d76a8f .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # compute the ROC curve (keeping every threshold, like pROC): fpr, tpr, roc_thresholds = roc_curve(test_data["presAbs"], pred_probs, drop_intermediate=False) # smoothed (binormal) version: a straight line on the probit scale finite = (fpr > 0) & (fpr < 1) & (tpr > 0) & (tpr < 1) # norm.ppf(0) and norm.ppf(1) are infinite slope, intercept_sm = np.polyfit(norm.ppf(tpr[finite]), norm.ppf(1 - fpr[finite]), deg=1) sens_smooth = np.linspace(0.0005, 0.9995, 500) spec_smooth = norm.cdf(intercept_sm + slope * norm.ppf(sens_smooth)) # bootstrap band: resample presences and absences separately (like pROC), 2000 times y_arr = test_data["presAbs"].to_numpy() p_arr = pred_probs.to_numpy() pres_idx = np.flatnonzero(y_arr == 1) abs_idx = np.flatnonzero(y_arr == 0) fpr_grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 101) rng = np.random.default_rng(2468) boot_tpr = [] for b in range(2000): idx = np.concatenate([rng.choice(pres_idx, size=len(pres_idx)), rng.choice(abs_idx, size=len(abs_idx))]) fpr_b, tpr_b, _ = roc_curve(y_arr[idx], p_arr[idx]) boot_tpr.append(np.interp(fpr_grid, fpr_b, tpr_b)) # sensitivity at each FPR on the grid lower, upper = np.percentile(boot_tpr, [2.5, 97.5], axis=0) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5)) ax.fill_between(fpr_grid, lower, upper, color="grey", alpha=0.3, label="95% bootstrap band") ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color="black", label="ROC curve") ax.plot(1 - spec_smooth, sens_smooth, color="blue", label="smoothed (binormal)") ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="lightgrey", lw=1) # a model with no skill (AUC = 0.5) ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate (1 - specificity)") ax.set_ylabel("True positive rate (sensitivity)") ax.set_aspect("equal") ax.legend(loc="lower right"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=439 height=431} ::: ::: The area under the curve (AUC) and a confidence interval for it. `sdm.auc_ci()` uses DeLong's method, the default of pROC's `ci()`, and returns three numbers: the lower limit, the AUC, and the upper limit. ::: {#f804a76e .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} roc_auc_score(test_data["presAbs"], pred_probs) # get the area under the curve ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` 0.8141372141372142 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4f4db457 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} sdm.auc_ci(test_data["presAbs"], pred_probs) # get a confidence interval for the AUC ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` (np.float64(0.7538813600057933), np.float64(0.8141372141372142), np.float64(0.874393068268635)) ``` ::: ::: pROC's `coords(x = "best")` reports the "best" point on the curve: by default, the threshold that maximizes sensitivity + specificity (Youden's J, which is the TSS). `np.argmax()` finds the position of the largest value. (pROC reports thresholds halfway between adjacent predicted values, while scikit-learn reports the predicted values themselves, so the threshold numbers differ slightly. Sensitivity and specificity are the same.) ::: {#9e819f7e .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} best = np.argmax(tpr - fpr) # TPR - FPR = sensitivity + specificity - 1 print(f"threshold = {roc_thresholds[best]:.4f}") print(f"specificity = {1 - fpr[best]:.4f}") print(f"sensitivity = {tpr[best]:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` threshold = 0.2760 specificity = 0.7189 sensitivity = 0.8000 ``` ::: ::: Partial ROC curves were mentioned by Lobo et al (2008) as an alternative to AUC. pROC calculates these through its `auc()` function. scikit-learn has no direct equivalent for a range like this, but we can compute it ourselves: the area under the ROC curve for specificity between 0.3 and 0.7, i.e., FPR between 0.3 and 0.7. We read the curve's sensitivity off at many closely spaced FPR values (`np.interp()`) and add up the area with the trapezoid rule (`auc()`). Like pROC's default, this is the raw (un-standardized) partial area, so the largest possible value is 0.4, the width of the range. ::: {#a56b267e .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} # AUC clipped to specificity between 0.3 and 0.7 fpr_range = np.linspace(0.3, 0.7, 2001) partial_auc = auc(fpr_range, np.interp(fpr_range, fpr, tpr)) partial_auc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` 0.35463846153846146 ``` ::: ::: Sensitivity and specificity are not the only metrics that trade-off as the threshold changes. We can also look at precision and recall, with precision-recall curves. Like R's PRROC plot, we color the curve by threshold. As a one-number summary, scikit-learn reports the *average precision*, which is close to, but not exactly the same as, PRROC's area under the PR curve (they connect the points of the curve differently). ::: {#171a3d00 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} precision, recall, pr_thresholds = precision_recall_curve(test_data["presAbs"], pred_probs) ap = average_precision_score(test_data["presAbs"], pred_probs) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5)) ax.plot(recall, precision, color="lightgrey", zorder=1) points = ax.scatter(recall[:-1], precision[:-1], c=pr_thresholds, s=10, zorder=2) fig.colorbar(points, ax=ax, label="threshold") ax.set_xlabel("Recall (sensitivity)") ax.set_ylabel("Precision (positive predictive value)") ax.set_xlim(0, 1) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_title(f"PR curve; average precision = {ap:.3f}"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=548 height=451} ::: ::: Thought experiment: Suppose that your study extent is much larger than necessary - imagine a species endemic to Oregon but with surveys across North America. We can approximate this by adding more negatives to the dataset. Suppose these are 'easy' negatives, so the model predicts a very low probability of occurrence at all of them - say, 0.0001. The new data are: ::: {#88cb50b9 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} n_new_points = 1000 new_obs = np.concatenate([test_data["presAbs"], np.zeros(n_new_points)]) new_preds = np.concatenate([pred_probs, np.full(n_new_points, 0.0001)]) ``` ::: > **Exercise 2:** Plot the original ROC and PR curves, and add new curves to the plots for the data > augmented with easily-predicted negatives. What do you notice? # PART 2: CROSS-VALIDATION # Models To Fit We'll fit many logistic regressions below, so let's write two small functions: one to fit a model with a given list of variables, and one to predict probabilities from it. We'll also collect each set of results in a *dictionary* (`roc_results`), keyed by a label, so one function can redraw all the ROC curves so far. `for label, (y, p) in roc_results.items():` loops over the dictionary's labels and values. ::: {#5c3c3fc0 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} def fit_glm(variables, data): """Fit a logistic regression (binomial GLM) of presAbs on the given variables.""" return sm.GLM(data["presAbs"], sm.add_constant(data[variables]), family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit() def predict_glm(model, variables, data): """Predicted probabilities of presence for the rows of `data`.""" return model.predict(sm.add_constant(data[variables])) roc_results = {} # label -> (true labels, predictions) roc_colors = {"true": "black", "resub": "red", "random": "orange", "long": "green", "grid": "blue"} def plot_rocs(results): """Draw the ROC curve for every entry of `results` on one plot.""" fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5)) ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="lightgrey", lw=1) for label, (y, p) in results.items(): fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, p) ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color=roc_colors[label], lw=2, label=label) ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate (1 - specificity)") ax.set_ylabel("True positive rate (sensitivity)") ax.set_aspect("equal") ax.legend(loc="lower right") def print_auc(y, p): """Print the AUC and its DeLong 95% confidence interval.""" lower, auc_value, upper = sdm.auc_ci(y, p) print(f"AUC = {auc_value:.4f} 95% CI: {lower:.4f} - {upper:.4f} (DeLong)") ``` ::: As a benchmark, let's look at the true model that generated the data, fit to all the data and evaluated on all the data (resubstitution). This is basically as well as we can hope to do, and note that it is not actually perfect, due to the inherent stochasticity/noise. ::: {#5415f03c .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} # fit the true model on all the data: true_vars = ["Precipitation.Seasonality", "Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter"] true_model = fit_glm(true_vars, modeling_df) # evaluate with resubstitution: preds_true = predict_glm(true_model, true_vars, modeling_df) roc_results["true"] = (modeling_df["presAbs"], preds_true) print_auc(modeling_df["presAbs"], preds_true) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC = 0.8626 95% CI: 0.8289 - 0.8962 (DeLong) ``` ::: ::: Since in the real world we always have some degree of model misspecification, let's use a slightly wrong model for the rest of our exploration. Suppose we fail to include Precipitation.Seasonality (variable 15) in the model, and include Precipitation.of.Driest.Month (variable 14) instead. Let's see how that model does, again using resubstitution. The gap between these is the price we pay for model misspecification in this case. ::: {#de7b637f .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} # suppose we do NOT specify the model correctly: model_vars = ["Min.Temperature.of.Coldest.Month", "Mean.Temperature.of.Wettest.Quarter", "Precipitation.of.Driest.Month"] # resubstitution: mod_resub = fit_glm(model_vars, modeling_df) preds_resub = predict_glm(mod_resub, model_vars, modeling_df) roc_results["resub"] = (modeling_df["presAbs"], preds_resub) print_auc(modeling_df["presAbs"], preds_resub) plot_rocs(roc_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC = 0.8305 95% CI: 0.7919 - 0.8691 (DeLong) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-23-output-2.png){width=439 height=431} ::: ::: # Train/Test Splits Now, instead of resubstitution, let's use some different splitting methods to divide the data into a training set and a test set. A small function draws each split on a map. ::: {#4bf1380d .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} def plot_split(train, test): """Map the training (purple) and test (gray) points over the first environmental layer.""" ax = sdm.plot_map(env_stack["Annual.Mean.Temperature"], env_stack, title="Annual.Mean.Temperature") ax.scatter(train["x"], train["y"], s=8, color="purple", label="training") ax.scatter(test["x"], test["y"], s=8, color="gray", label="test") ax.legend(loc="lower left") ``` ::: First, let's divide the points randomly in half. `rng.choice()` picks row positions at random (without replacement), and `.drop()` removes those rows to leave the test set. ::: {#dffccc3b .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(12345) samp = rng.choice(n_points, size=round(0.5 * n_points), replace=False) traindata = modeling_df.iloc[samp] testdata = modeling_df.drop(modeling_df.index[samp]) # visualize the split: purple training set and gray test set plot_split(traindata, testdata) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-25-output-1.png){width=529 height=293} ::: ::: Fit the model to these training data, predict on the test data, and evaluate with ROC. ::: {#e20ac8f8 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} mod_rand = fit_glm(model_vars, traindata) preds_rand = predict_glm(mod_rand, model_vars, testdata) roc_results["random"] = (testdata["presAbs"], preds_rand) print_auc(testdata["presAbs"], preds_rand) plot_rocs(roc_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC = 0.8052 95% CI: 0.7454 - 0.8651 (DeLong) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-26-output-2.png){width=439 height=431} ::: ::: Next, let's split the data in half longitudinally, based on the median longitude among the observed points. ::: {#b940358b .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} mid_long = modeling_df["x"].median() train_idxs = modeling_df["x"] >= mid_long traindata = modeling_df[train_idxs] test_idxs = modeling_df["x"] < mid_long testdata = modeling_df[test_idxs] # visualize the split: purple training set and gray test set plot_split(traindata, testdata) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-27-output-1.png){width=529 height=293} ::: ::: Repeat the model fitting and evaluation procedures on this split: ::: {#2bcce346 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} mod_half = fit_glm(model_vars, traindata) preds_half = predict_glm(mod_half, model_vars, testdata) roc_results["long"] = (testdata["presAbs"], preds_half) print_auc(testdata["presAbs"], preds_half) plot_rocs(roc_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC = 0.7066 95% CI: 0.6301 - 0.7832 (DeLong) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-28-output-2.png){width=439 height=431} ::: ::: Splitting longitudinally might produce two dissimilar datasets (e.g., the elevation distribution across the two may be different). A variety of grid-based partitionings might result in more similar samples from the environmental space. Here, we can try just a 2x2 grid, with the opposing corners put into the same subset. (`|` means "or".) ::: {#9fe0dc0b .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} mid_lat = modeling_df["y"].median() train_idxs = (((modeling_df["x"] >= mid_long) & (modeling_df["y"] >= mid_lat)) | ((modeling_df["x"] < mid_long) & (modeling_df["y"] < mid_lat))) traindata = modeling_df[train_idxs] test_idxs = (((modeling_df["x"] < mid_long) & (modeling_df["y"] >= mid_lat)) | ((modeling_df["x"] >= mid_long) & (modeling_df["y"] < mid_lat))) testdata = modeling_df[test_idxs] # assign to training and test: plot_split(traindata, testdata) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-29-output-1.png){width=529 height=293} ::: ::: Repeat the modeling fitting and evaluation. ::: {#812f030a .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} mod_grid = fit_glm(model_vars, traindata) preds_grid = predict_glm(mod_grid, model_vars, testdata) roc_results["grid"] = (testdata["presAbs"], preds_grid) print_auc(testdata["presAbs"], preds_grid) plot_rocs(roc_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC = 0.8190 95% CI: 0.7678 - 0.8702 (DeLong) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-30-output-2.png){width=439 height=431} ::: ::: > **Question 1:** Reflect on this set of simulations. What changes > would have DECREASED the differences? [Note: I consider these questions to be nontrivial, so > don't be intimidated if you don't have a complete explanation for everything! Please just give > this some careful thought and share what you come up with.] # K-fold cross-validation The process above splits the data into one training set and one test set. An alternative is to split the data into $k$ sets, or 'folds,' and let each take a turn as the test set, using a model trained on everything else. The example below illustrates this process using scikit-learn's `StratifiedKFold`. In addition to splitting into $k$ folds, this time, we'll stratify the folds by prevalence. `skf.split()` hands back the row positions of the training and test points for one fold at a time. `enumerate(..., start=1)` also counts the folds (1, 2, ...) as we loop, and `_` is the usual name for a value we don't need. We use the loop to record each point's fold number. ::: {#1e4ffa85 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} k = 5 # StratifiedKFold keeps about the same proportion of presences in every fold skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=4321) fold_assgn = np.zeros(n_points, dtype=int) for fold, (_, test_positions) in enumerate(skf.split(modeling_df, modeling_df["presAbs"]), start=1): fold_assgn[test_positions] = fold print(pd.crosstab(fold_assgn, modeling_df["presAbs"], rownames=["fold"])) # plot the folds, each in a different color fold_colors = plt.cm.hsv(np.linspace(0, 1, k, endpoint=False)) # like R's rainbow(k) ax = sdm.plot_map(env_stack["Annual.Mean.Temperature"], env_stack, title="Annual.Mean.Temperature") for f in range(1, k + 1): in_fold = fold_assgn == f ax.scatter(modeling_df.loc[in_fold, "x"], modeling_df.loc[in_fold, "y"], s=8, color=fold_colors[f - 1], label=f"fold {f}") ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` presAbs 0 1 fold 1 72 28 2 72 28 3 72 28 4 73 27 5 73 27 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-31-output-2.png){width=529 height=293} ::: ::: Here, we iterate over the folds, letting each take its turn as the test set while we train on all the others. In each case, we can record the test predictions to aggregate later and/or measure performance for the test fold individually. ::: {#ff8c0dbf .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} # set up an array to store the test metric for each fold fold_aucs = np.zeros(k) # also collect all the predictions into a single array # (this array will be filled bit by bit over the k folds) cv_preds = np.zeros(n_points) # loop over the folds, training on NOT this fold and testing on this fold for f in range(1, k + 1): in_fold = (fold_assgn == f) mod_f = fit_glm(model_vars, modeling_df[~in_fold]) pred_f = predict_glm(mod_f, model_vars, modeling_df[in_fold]) cv_preds[in_fold] = pred_f fold_aucs[f - 1] = roc_auc_score(modeling_df["presAbs"][in_fold], pred_f) # we can get a single AUC from the vector of predictions we collected over the folds print_auc(modeling_df["presAbs"], cv_preds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AUC = 0.8269 95% CI: 0.7879 - 0.8659 (DeLong) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#e65a0f26 .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} # or we can average the individual AUCs over the folds print(fold_aucs) print(fold_aucs.mean()) print(fold_aucs.std(ddof=1)) # ddof=1 gives the sample standard deviation, like R's sd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [0.80803571 0.79315476 0.84126984 0.87417555 0.81684424] 0.8266960208741031 0.031768625021215205 ``` ::: ::: > **Exercise 3:** Try this with a few different numbers of folds. Report on your observations. What > are some considerations that might guide your choice of the number of folds? # BONUS SECTION (optional): BlockCV Those of you that are particularly interested in structured CV may wish to explore spatial blocking. In R, the blockCV package (Valavi et al. 2019) builds spatial blocks (squares or hexagons of a chosen size), assigns whole blocks to folds, and can estimate the range of spatial autocorrelation in the predictors to help choose the block size. There is no equivalent package in our Python toolkit, but the core idea is easy to build ourselves as a stand-in: 1. Cut the map into square blocks of `block_size` degrees and give each point the ID of its block. 2. Use scikit-learn's `GroupKFold`, which puts all points of a group (here, a block) in the same fold. Some differences from blockCV: the R version uses 500 km hexagons and assigns blocks to folds at random (keeping the most even of 50 tries), while `GroupKFold` assigns blocks so that the folds have similar numbers of points, with no randomness. Also, a degree of longitude gets shorter toward the poles, so our "square" blocks are narrower (in km) in the north. ::: {#fa68249e .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} block_size = 5 # degrees; 5 degrees of latitude is about 550 km block_col = np.floor(modeling_df["x"] / block_size).astype(int) block_row = np.floor(modeling_df["y"] / block_size).astype(int) block_id = block_col.astype(str) + "_" + block_row.astype(str) # e.g. "-25_9" print(block_id.nunique(), "blocks contain points") gkf = GroupKFold(n_splits=5) spatial_folds = np.zeros(n_points, dtype=int) for fold, (_, test_positions) in enumerate(gkf.split(modeling_df, groups=block_id), start=1): spatial_folds[test_positions] = fold print(pd.crosstab(spatial_folds, modeling_df["presAbs"], rownames=["fold"])) ax = sdm.plot_map(env_stack["Annual.Mean.Temperature"], env_stack, title="Spatial blocks", cmap="Greys", colorbar=False) for f in range(1, 6): in_fold = spatial_folds == f ax.scatter(modeling_df.loc[in_fold, "x"], modeling_df.loc[in_fold, "y"], s=8, color=fold_colors[f - 1], label=f"fold {f}") ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-170, -45, block_size), minor=True) # draw the block edges ax.set_yticks(np.arange(5, 75, block_size), minor=True) ax.grid(which="minor", color="grey", linewidth=0.3) ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8); # spatial_folds holds the fold number of each point, like fold_assgn above ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 154 blocks contain points presAbs 0 1 fold 1 77 23 2 68 32 3 80 20 4 69 31 5 68 32 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-34-output-2.png){width=566 height=348} ::: ::: blockCV's `cv_spatial_autocor()` estimates how far apart two places must be before the environmental values stop being similar (the *range* of spatial autocorrelation), by fitting a variogram to each layer. As a simpler look at the same idea, here is an *empirical semivariogram* for the three variables in the true model: for pairs of random cells, half the average squared difference in a variable, plotted against the distance between the cells. Where a curve levels off is roughly the autocorrelation range. (This takes a few seconds: 2,000 cells make about 2 million pairs.) ::: {#652b6746 .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} cells = env_stack.sample_random(2000, seed=97531) lon = np.radians(cells["x"].to_numpy()) lat = np.radians(cells["y"].to_numpy()) pairs = np.triu_indices(len(cells), k=1) # every pair of cells, counted once i, j = pairs # great-circle distance between the two cells of each pair, in km (the haversine formula) a = (np.sin((lat[i] - lat[j]) / 2) ** 2 + np.cos(lat[i]) * np.cos(lat[j]) * np.sin((lon[i] - lon[j]) / 2) ** 2) dist_km = 2 * 6371 * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(a)) bins = np.arange(0, 4001, 100) # 100 km distance classes bin_of_pair = np.digitize(dist_km, bins) bin_mid = bins[:-1] + 50 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4)) for name in true_vars: z = cells[name].to_numpy() half_sq_diff = 0.5 * (z[i] - z[j]) ** 2 semivariance = [half_sq_diff[bin_of_pair == b].mean() for b in range(1, len(bins))] ax.plot(bin_mid, semivariance, marker=".", label=name) ax.set_xlabel("Distance between cells (km)") ax.set_ylabel("Semivariance") ax.legend(fontsize=8); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](lab02-evaluation_files/figure-html/cell-35-output-1.png){width=590 height=359} ::: ::: Over a whole continent, a variable that changes along a broad gradient (like minimum temperature, which rises steadily from north to south) keeps increasing with distance and never levels off. blockCV runs into the same thing: its fitted ranges for such layers can be implausibly large. So choosing a block size takes judgment, not just a formula. # Turn in **(a Canvas discussion post, by the due date on Canvas)** Please post to the online discussion of this lab.
